items.title: JetBlue raises baggage fees for a second time as jet fuel prices stay elevated
items.description: JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year, making it more expensive for travellers to check luggage just as the busy holiday travel season gets underway.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A Jet Blue Airlines jet pushes back from a gate at the Pittsburgh International Airport in Imperial, Pa., Feb. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Gene J. Puskar</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year, making it more expensive for travellers to check luggage just as the busy holiday travel season gets underway.
items.body:
JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year, making it more expensive for travellers to check luggage just as the busy holiday travel season gets underway.

The new fees for tickets purchased on or after Nov. 3 mean most economy passengers flying within the United States, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean will pay at least US$50 each way for their first checked bag, up from US$39 previously.

The price climbs to US$55 during peak travel periods, including Thanksgiving and the winter holidays, if passengers pay at least 24 hours before departure. Those who wait until the final 24 hours will pay US$60 during off-peak periods and US$70 during peak periods.

“We’re adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs,” JetBlue said in an emailed statement. “This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one.”

At the start of the year, the first checked bag on most economy domestic JetBlue flights cost US$35 during off-peak periods. But that was before the Iran war started in late February with U.S.-Israeli strikes and sent jet fuel prices swinging.

The fee for a second checked bag has also increased, starting at US$70 each way during off-peak periods and US$75 during peak travel. Passengers checking their bags at the airport can pay as much as US$85 for a second bag.

JetBlue, which has its flagship terminal at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, previously raised checked baggage fees in March. That increase helped set off a broader round of baggage fee hikes among major U.S. airlines, including Delta, United, American and Southwest.

The war with Iran remains unresolved, keeping traffic largely restricted through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route for global oil supplies. The disruption has kept jet fuel prices elevated.

JetBlue executives said last week during the airline’s third-quarter earnings call that demand has remained resilient even as fares have risen in response to higher jet fuel prices. JetBlue said its average fuel price reached US$3.91 per gallon in the summer, up 57 per cent from a year earlier, and is expected to climb to US$4.64 during the final three months of the year, up 85 per cent from the same time last year.

JetBlue said some travellers, including eligible co-branded credit card holders and members of JetBlue’s loyalty program, can still check bags for free.

Rio Yamat, The Associated Press

items.title: How much further diesel prices need to fall before Canadian consumers see relief at the grocery store
items.description: The cost of diesel went down 13 cents in many parts of Nova Scotia on Wednesday morning to 256.5 cents a litre, with similar price drops across the country.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The cost of diesel went down 13 cents a litre in many parts of Nova Scotia on Tuesday morning. (CTV News/Paul Hollingsworth)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The cost of diesel went down 13 cents in many parts of Nova Scotia on Wednesday morning to 256.5 cents a litre, with similar price drops across the country.
items.body:
ENFIELD, N.S. - The cost of diesel went down 13 cents in many parts of Nova Scotia on Wednesday morning to 256.5 cents a litre, with similar price drops across the country.

Regular self-serve gasoline was also cheaper in several provinces, including an 11 cent drop in Toronto, which brought gas prices to $1.67 a litre.

“It is fantastic and hopefully it’s a sign of more things to come,” said Colin MacDonald as he filled up his pickup truck with diesel at the truck stop in Enfield, N.S. “A lot of people are struggling and just doing what they can to get by so I’m sure this is going to make a lot of people happy.”

Trucker Roger Spicer said it added up to major savings as he filled up his massive work truck.

“I think the diesel savings today will be about $60,” said Spicer, who added the decreased price was welcome news at a time when everything is getting more expensive. “I am the same as everybody else, going to the grocery store, even filling up your car with gas, it all costs a lot.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

According to analyst Carol Montreuil, the lower fuel prices are a reaction to global market optimism about the wars involving Iran and Ukraine.

“There is still no resolution, but there are hopes for it,” said Montreuil, who is a vice-president with the Canadian Fuels Association. “This is really reflecting on the price of crude, which has come down significantly in the past couple of days and that is great news for consumers.”

Montreuil said the North American economy is largely fuelled by diesel. Growing energy and transportation costs have been passed on to Canadians who have been forced to pay more for everyday purchases.

“People have seen the prices of everything go up and that includes the prices of that food and transportation,” said Montreuil. “The impact is being felt in all sectors including agriculture.”

Dalhousie University professor and food researcher Sylvain Charlebois pointed out Canada’s food inflation rate in September was 2.2 per cent, but if shoppers were hoping lower diesel prices would lead to more affordable groceries, they will be disappointed, at least in the short term.

“Everything that is hauled in is based on contracts that were signed a few months ago,” said Charlebois. “Seeing fuel prices drop is a really good sign but those prices need to remain low for a while.”

Montreuil said the focus will now be on U.S. President Donald Trump.

Now with the U.S. midterm elections over, he wonders whether sweeping losses for Republicans would affect Trump’s policies regarding the wars with Iran and Ukraine, which would have an impact on fuel supplies around the world.

items.body:
In a sweeping upset to U.S. President Donald Trump’s power in Washington, the Democrats have retaken control of the American legislative branch.

Democrats won control of the Senate and Congress, in a widespread rebuke of Trump and the Republican Party, The Associated Press reported.

Two years deep into a trade war, Canadians wait to see the impacts of the shift in the balance of power, but on Wednesday it remained unclear how the results will impact trade negotiations.

The two sides have yet to come to an agreement, and while Prime Minister Mark Carney indicated progress, political watchers say immediate relief is unlikely.

items.title: Lockheed Martin to pay US$29.5M to settle federal claims it discriminated against white workers
items.description: Defence contractor Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay US$29.5 million to settle claims that it discriminated against white workers.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A person tests out a flight simulator for the Lockheed Martin F-35 multirole combat aircraft at the Canadian Association of Defence and Security Industries annual defence industry trade show CANSEC in Ottawa on May 27, 2026. (Justin Tang / The Canadian Press)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Defence contractor Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay US$29.5 million to settle claims that it discriminated against white workers.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Defence contractor Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay US$29.5 million to settle claims by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration that it discriminated against white workers through its efforts to promote diversity and equity in an internal bonus program.

Lockheed Martin will pay US$22 million to the U.S. government to resolve claims that it failed to comply with anti-discrimination requirements in its federal contracts, according to the settlement announced Wednesday by the Justice Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

In addition, Lockheed Martin will pay US$7.5 million to more than 1,000 affected employees as part of a settlement with the EEOC, which had been investigating the company for violating Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act, which prohibits employment discrimination based on race.

In a statement, Lockheed Martin denied the government’s allegations but said it “agreed to resolve this matter with the Department of Justice and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to avoid the distraction and expense of prolonged litigation.”

“We did not admit liability, determining it would be best for all involved to put these matters behind us so we can remain focused on our critical national security mission,” the company said.

The case is the latest example of the Trump administration’s use of the 1863 False Claims Act to pressure federal contractors into abandoning diversity, equity and inclusion practices. The law states that contractors that make false claims to the government could be liable for extensive damages. Typically used to police fraud, the Trump administration has invoked the False Claims Act against companies it maintains have pursued discriminatory practices under the guise of promoting diversity.

The Justice Department has reached similar settlements with IBM, Deloitte and Accenture.

Civil rights groups have criticized the Trump administration’s policies for taking aim at many long-established practices that are aimed at ensuring the hiring, promotion and other employment practices do not intentionally or unintentionally discriminate against traditionally marginalized groups. Several groups have filed lawsuits against the Trump administration’s anti-DEI policies.

The allegations against Lockheed Martin center around a program the company introduced in 2021 to give the top 20% of employees a merit-based salary bump and promotion opportunities, according to the settlement agreement.

Managers submitted nominations for the bonuses, which the company then ran through an analysis to “flag” statistical outliers based on the race and sex composition of the list. If the nomination list raised flags, managers were asked to review their nominations and the “merit-based basis for the selections, without asking them to take any protected characteristic into account.”

But in practice, according to the Justice Department, Lockheed Martin personnel “exerted pressure on leaders in their business group to resolve race-related ‘flags’ by directing them to add or remove particular employees based on race.” The Justice Department claimed the managers were asked to remove nonminorities from the selections and add racial minorities.

The settlement with the DOJ and the EEOC stems from complaints made by Tim Booher, a former vice president at Lockheed Martin, who will be paid US$4.4 million by the U.S. government under a whistleblower provision of the False Claims Act. According to a complaint he filed in federal court in October 2025, Booher resigned from Lockheed Martin in May 2023 because he “felt that he could no longer be complicit in LMC’s illegal discrimination.”

In July 2024, Booher said he met with EEOC Commissioner Andrea Lucas to detail his allegations against the company. Lucas, who was elevated to EEOC chair after Trump took office in January 2025, filed a commissioner’s charge against Lockheed Martin, triggering the EEOC’s investigation.

Attorneys representing Booher released a statement applauding the “amicable conclusion that avoids prolonged litigation and ensures statutory compliance in federal contracting.”

Lucas, a vehement critic of DEI practices, has publicly urged white men to come to the EEOC with discrimination complaints and has filed her own “commissioner’s charges” against the diversity practices of companies, including Nike.

“Title VII protects every worker from employment discrimination on the basis of race — and that protection does not yield when discriminatory decisions are framed as diversity initiatives,” Lucas said in a statement announcing the settlement.

Alexandra Olson, The Associated Press

items.title: Ontario court certifies class-action suit against TD Bank regarding money laundering
items.description: An Ontario court has certified a class-action lawsuit against TD Bank and certain members of its senior leadership team including former CEO Bharat Masrani in relation to its anti-money laundering program.

items._ogDesc: An Ontario court has certified a class-action lawsuit against TD Bank and certain members of its senior leadership team including former CEO Bharat Masrani in relation to its anti-money laundering program.
items.body:
TORONTO — An Ontario court has certified a class-action lawsuit against TD Bank and certain members of its senior leadership team including former CEO Bharat Masrani in relation to its anti-money laundering program.

The lawsuit alleges that the lender misrepresented long-standing deficiencies in the program between 2021 and 2024 and prioritized profits over regulatory compliance.

TD was fined more than US$3 billion by U.S. regulators in 2024 after pleading guilty to multiple charges related to failures in the program.

The lawsuit says those failures led to its subsidiaries becoming the first banks in U.S. history to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering.

According to the lawsuit, that caused significant investor losses when the company’s market capitalization dropped by $30 billion.

The defendants in the lawsuit deny the allegations, and TD Bank did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

items.title: China-Canada trade agreement extended to late 2028
items.description: Beijing and Ottawa are extending  an agreement to provide Chinese market access to Canadian imports and Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A deer leaps through a canola field as another stands nearby, in Fort St. John, B.C., on Tuesday, July 14, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Darryl Dyck]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">DARRYL DYCK</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Beijing and Ottawa are extending  an agreement to provide Chinese market access to Canadian imports and Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Beijing and Ottawa are extending a January agreement to provide Chinese market access to Canadian imports in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

The news comes as one of China’s most important officials prepares to visit Vancouver and Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to return to China later this month.

In March, China dropped tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab. Canada agreed in return to allow in certain Chinese steel and aluminum products.

The deal was negotiated by Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping during a visit to China. It was set to expire at the end of this year.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

On Wednesday, Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said the deal is being extended by two years, to the end of 2028.

“This extension gives Canadian farmers, producers and harvesters stable access to China and supports billions in export opportunities,” Sidhu said in a news release.

He said the credit goes to a trade body Canada and China relaunched in January as Ottawa moved to increase exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030.

Sidhu was in Beijing for meetings with officials ahead of Carney’s planned visit to China’s tech city Shenzhen later this month for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit.

“The timing of the announcement is significant,” said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, in an emailed statement.

She said the clearing of “an immediate trade irritant” allows Carney to focus on boosting Chinese investment during his visit to Shenzhen. It also locks in Chinese steel and aluminum access, which she said will be a factor in Ottawa’s trade talks with Washington.

“Ottawa is increasingly having to navigate its economic relationships with Beijing and Washington simultaneously, and decisions made in one relationship inevitably have implications for the other,” she wrote.

On Wednesday, Ottawa announced that Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng will visit Vancouver on Sunday and Monday.

Though he is not China’s trade or finance minister, Lifeng plays a major role in crafting Beijing’s trade and economic polices.

Sidhu and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will welcome He and events are also planned with Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem and financial regulators.

Sidhu’s office said Wednesday the canola news stems from months of efforts to improve trade relations with China.

In June 2025, Sidhu said he and Wang Wentao, China’s minister of commerce, agreed to restart a joint economic and trade commission to address trade issues. In January, he said Ottawa secured a preliminary joint arrangement in Beijing which opened up more than $7 billion in market space for Canadian workers and businesses.

Sidhu said that since the arrangement took effect in March, canola seed exports to China have increased by 84 per cent, from $1.04 billion to $1.91 billion, compared to the same period last year.

He said canola meal exports more than doubled, from $146 million to $390 million, while pea exports grew from $107 million to $345 million. Sidhu also said lobster exports increased by 57 per cent, from $128 million to $200 million.

Warren Kaeding, Saskatchewan’s trade minister, told reporters in Regina that farmers are pleased with the deal.

“That helps so much in them being able to plan their cropping rotations into next year,” he said. “(They’re) going into the spring with a bit of confidence that they at least have a two-year extension on tariff reductions on canola and peas.”

Canadian beef also returned to the Chinese market in January for the first time since 2021, said Sidhu. From January to August, he said, Canada sent $363.2 million in beef exports to China, nearly double what it sold there in all of 2021.

“Over the past year, I’ve met with industry representatives, including the Canola Council of Canada, Pulse Canada, the Fisheries Council of Canada, the Canadian Cattle Association and the Canadian Meat Council,” says a media statement from Sidhu’s office.

“They told me an extension would give them the predictable, long-term access to the Chinese market and the certainty they need. We listened, and we delivered.”

Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said on social media the extension provides “immediate certainty” for lobster and crab harvesters and exporters. She said discussions are continuing on other seafood products.

“Last week in China, I met with government officials and industry leaders to make the case for Canada as a trusted supplier,” she said. “Canada’s fish and seafood harvesters catch the best seafood in the world and their work drives rural and coastal communities across the country.”

In Beijing earlier this year, Carney outlined steps to build a new strategic partnership with China, including more cultural exchanges and “people-to-people” ties.

Carney said during his visit that Ottawa hoped the renewal would become an “example to the world of co-operation amidst a time globally of division and disorder.”

Culture Minister Marc Miller made a five-day trip to China last month with dozens of representatives from Canadian creative industries. His office said seven new commercial agreements worth more than $4.2 million were signed during the trip.

The Carney government is seeking to double non-U.S. exports in the next decade in response to the unstable geopolitical and trading environment ushered in by the re-election of U.S. President Donald Trump.

China is Canada’s second largest single-country merchandise trading partner, accounting for $125.7 billion in two-way merchandise trade in 2025.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

items.title: Suncor seeking new ways to deliver fuel around the globe: CEO
items.description: Suncor’s exports of refined products are up 80 per cent so far this year as the oilsands giant finds unconventional ways to deliver fuel to thirsty markets.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Suncor Energy Centre is pictured in downtown Calgary, Alta., Friday, Sept. 16, 2022. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Jeff McIntosh]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff McIntosh</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Suncor’s exports of refined products are up 80 per cent so far this year as the oilsands giant finds unconventional ways to deliver fuel to thirsty markets.
items.body:
CALGARY — Suncor’s exports of refined products are up 80 per cent so far this year as the oilsands giant finds unconventional ways to deliver fuel to thirsty markets around the globe facing supply disruptions from Russia and the Middle East. 

“This has been a really fun area,” chief executive officer Rich Kruger told analysts on a conference call Wednesday to discuss third-quarter results. 

In the past, looking to sell products like diesel and jet fuel internationally was seen as a “last resort,” he added. 

  • Latest updates on company news here

“You get your barrel there because you don’t have a better home for it. Those markets now have been particularly valuable because of acute shortages.”

Suncor has access to nine time charters, an arrangement where a ship can be leased for a set period, said Dave Oldreive, Suncor’s vice-president in charge of the company’s refining and sales segments. They can be used to transport crude, or high-demand products made from it. 

Rates were locked in before a recent spike in global freight costs, which has been one driver behind a widening in the discount on Canadian heavy oil. 

“We’re seeing massive savings relative to current spot freight rates,” Oldreive said. 

Kruger said the time-charter arrangements will be in place “well into next year,” though the exact terms can’t be divulged because they’re proprietary.

“Sometimes we’d rather be lucky than good,” he said. “We took a lot of these actions not anticipating the unique benefits we see now, but they have been extremely valuable for us. And I think in the quarters ahead, they’re going to continue to be.”

In addition to the West Coast, Suncor has also found ways to serve “niche markets” via the East Coast, like Scandinavia and Iceland. Product has also found eager buyers in Central America, Oldreive added. 

Year-to-date, Suncor has been able to export 75,000 barrels a day of refined product. Total refined product sales in the third quarter hit a record 677,000 barrels a day, up from 647,000 barrels a day in the same period a year earlier.  

Last month, Suncor announced a deal to sell its interest in three oil developments off the shores of Newfoundland for $1.2 billion to U.K.-based Ithaca Energy PLC as it focuses more of its capital and attention on its core oilsands business. 

“These assets — certainly of value — frankly were not in that family photo,” Kruger said of its stakes in Terra Nova, White Rose and West White Rose. 

“In Ithaca, we found a buyer whose strategy and core competency is aligned with these assets and consequently was willing to pay us accordingly — win-win for both parties.” 

  • Sign up for breaking news alerts from CTV News, right at your fingertips

Suncor does still maintain some presence off the East Coast, choosing to keep its non-operated interests in the Hebron and Hibernia fields. ExxonMobil Canada operates Hebron and is lead owner in Hibernia.

“A big part of who’s in the family photo and how close you snuggle up to me and my wife is, what do you bring to the party? And can we add value to what you do?” Kruger said. 

“Hebron and Hibernia bring a lot to the party: their longer life, their stable operation, a rock-solid operator who knows how to operate in the offshore quite well. Fundamentally, we cash dividend cheques each month from them and they run it really well.”

Late Tuesday, Suncor reported net earnings of $3.8 billion during the third quarter, up from $1.6 billion during the same period last year. 

On a per share basis, its profit amounted to $3.27, compared with $1.34 during the prior-year quarter. 

  • The information you need to know, sent directly to you: Download the CTV News App

Adjusted operating earnings, which Suncor considers a better gauge of its underlying performance because it filters out the effects of unusual items, were $4.6 billion, or $3.97 per share. 

That’s up from last year’s third quarter, when Suncor had adjusted operating earnings of $1.8 billion, or $1.48 per share. 

Total upstream production was 852,500 barrels per day in the third quarter, down year-over-year from 870,000 

Subsequent to its third quarter, Suncor’s board of directors approved a dividend increase of 10 per cent to 66 cents per common share.

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items.title: Repealing B.C. housing legislation would be a mistake, says UBC expert
items.description: VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.
items._ogDesc: VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.
items.body:
VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.

Alexandra Flynn, who teaches housing policy at the University of B.C., said the province still needs a lot of homes for low-to very-low-income residents, despite the thousands of empty units.

"We do have a number of empty condos, but market housing for above-average income earners is not the housing we need," she said. Left alone, the market cannot supply affordable and deeply affordable housing, she added.

"If you asked any developer, they would tell you, absent some kind of government intervention and granting and funding, they are not going to be able to do it."

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has promised to repeal key aspects of the provincial housing legislation introduced by the outgoing government of Premier David Eby.

"We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria," Doerkson said during the inaugural meeting of the Conservative caucus.

Doerkson was referring to the proposed repeal of Bill 44, which New Democrats consider their signature piece of housing legislation.

The legislation legalized higher densities on single-lot properties in municipalities with populations above 5,000 people, but also came with housing targets, which have been heavily criticized by local governments.

Sarrah Storey, president of the Union of the British Columbia Municipalities, said Bill 44 was "highly problematic" and municipalities pushed back because the government imposed it as a "one-size-fits-all model" without getting input.

Storey said UBCM agrees with the idea that housing policy for Williams Lake should not be made in Victoria, but if government wants to make changes to Bill 44, it should give municipalities choice.

"There are some local governments that will want to remain with the policies that are in place, allowing multiple homes on single family lots, for example, and they should be able to do so," she said.

Storey, who is the mayor for Fraser Lake, said any housing plan must also consider infrastructure needs.

"I say the best way to support developers is to ensure that the local governments can direct development to areas that are ready to support growth," she said.

Flynn disagrees with the plan to repeal, saying the law can be a "powerful tool," and while some of it needs to be fixed, it would be a mistake to just throw it away.

"If I was the new government, I would not be making any knee-jerk reactions right now," she said.

Flynn said she understands criticism from municipalities, saying there was "no question" that the dialogue between municipalities and Victoria must be improved.

"The province should not be dictating what municipalities do without actually engaging and having the bilateral relationships that are appropriate," Flynn said.

She said housing in British Columbia is in a better place now than it was in 2017 for lots of reasons.

They include the work of the non-profit housing sector, municipalities, the federal government, and the provincial government, she said.

"So, the NDP government introduced some of the most transformative housing reforms in Canada," she said.

Changing circumstances over time do not negate the fact that municipalities need to ensure affordable housing can be built in their communities, she said.

"This is not the time to be thinking about what to repeal," she said. "It's a time to set the course for a new agenda moving forward."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Wolfgang Depner, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days. Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days.

Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.

But with an official BC Assessment valuation of more than $1.7 million, the house appeared to represent a bargain when it sold for $825,000 at Vancouver's annual tax auction at city hall on Wednesday. It had a reserve price of just $72,051.

It was among more than 60 properties auctioned off in this year's City of Vancouver tax sale, set off by owners who have not paid their taxes for three years in a row, with the reserve, or upset prices, set at the amounts owed to the city.

If East Vancouver is not to your taste, then perhaps Point Grey Road? It's one of the most exclusive addresses in Canada, where neighbours include Lululemon billionaire Chip Wilson, whose $73-million home is the most valuable in B.C.

A few blocks down the road from Wilson are two side-by-side houses valued around $5 million and $6 million. They are steps from Jericho Beach and the Royal Vancouver Yacht Club, and sold for less than half their values at $2 million and $2.75 million respectively.

There is, of course, a catch.

After auction day, the current owners have a year to redeem their property by paying their taxes, resulting in a refund to the bidder — plus interest at the rate of six per cent, far in excess of government bond yields or bank interest.

Ron Usher, a retired notary public, said tax auctions are "not for the faint of heart or the inexperienced."

"I suspect some of these tax sales are more whoops than deliberate," Usher said, citing situations such as inheritances.

"You can imagine the law is very much structured to give the maximum possible opportunity for the owner to sort out the problem," Usher said.

Though a posting last week included 116 properties listed for auction, by the time it began at 10 a.m. Wednesday, only 66 remained. Owners of three more properties paid their taxes while the auction was ongoing and the homes were removed from the block.

Vancouverite Darius Wu attended the auction "mostly for fun, hoping I'd get a bargain."

The 30-year-old likened the auction to buying a lottery ticket, but better.

"In a lottery, you lose money no matter what. Here, I would say, the odds are probably one in a hundred. You don't lose any money, and if you win, it's still … pretty good."

It was Wu's first auction in Vancouver, but he ducked out before noon after concluding he wouldn't outbid others in attendance.

"I think there are way more serious people here," he said, noting many of the bids were climbing to around half of the property value listed. "You need a lot of cash to actually participate here."

As the auction dragged on, most of those who earlier jockeyed for a spot inside the chambers trickled out, with the attendees dwindling to about a dozen.

Among them was a man who cast winning bids on dozens of properties, including the home on Windsor Street. Though he declined an interview, he said he didn't expect to be transferred the properties — he would instead collect the interest.

Winning bids are secured by paying the upset price. If the original owner pays their overdue tax within a year, the bidder is refunded the upset price with interest of six per cent. But if it is not redeemed after a year, the bidder takes ownership after paying the balance of their bid within 30 days.

Sean Holden, a longtime Vancouver Realtor, called bidding at the auction "an exercise in futility."

He said he often steers clients away from the auction. When asked if he has ever attended himself, his response is quick.

"I wouldn't waste my time," he said through a chuckle.

Holden points out that tax auction sales that go through to completion are very rare.

But they do happen, both in Vancouver and other B.C. municipalities that conduct their auctions every September on properties with two years of unpaid taxes.

Three properties have changed hands in the last five years in Burnaby, while the City of Vancouver said in a statement that there "were only three instances in the last 10 years where a property changed hands from a tax sale."

"The property taxes on almost all properties have historically been paid within the one-year redemption period," the statement said.

The City of Vancouver tells potential buyers not to trespass, but recommends people do their own research before bidding, noting in a posting last week that it is not responsible for the condition or quality of the homes.

"Prospective purchasers are urged to research the properties and make all necessary inquiries to municipal and other government departments to determine the existence of any bylaws, restriction, charges or other conditions which may affect the value or suitability of the properties," it says.

Holden, who has been a Realtor in the city for about three decades, said that adds risk for the buyer.

"You don't know what condition it will be, and (if) the sellers are forced out by the bank, whether they knock holes in the wall or do other strange things. You're taking a huge risk," he said.

All properties auctioned on Wednesday received bids. Only one property was sold for the upset price, but that amounted to nearly $1 million.

The two properties listed for sale in Burnaby last year both went through to completion.

The minutes from the tax sale show the same person purchased both properties.

An empty 9,262-square-foot lot on Walker Avenue sold for the upset price of $845, while its assessed value is $37,700.

The other property, which had an upset price of $269, was sold to the same buyer for $5,000. That may be less of a bargain — the property measures just 94-square feet and has a valuation of $3,600.

The City of Burnaby confirmed both properties were transferred after the one-year redemption period expired.

The City of Kelowna said it had an average of "about three to four properties" sold at its auction over the past six years, but added that "actual transfers of ownership through this process are very rare."

"City staff recall the last transfer occurring around 2016/2017," a spokeswoman said in a statement.

Abbotsford did not auction any properties this year or in 2024, but in 2025, it had two properties on the block. One sale went through on what the city called "a small undeveloped piece of land."

The highest bidders from Wednesday's auction in Vancouver must pay the upset price by noon Thursday.

Holden said bidders need to be prepared for their money to be tied up for a while, noting that while a six per cent interest rate may be enticing, most owners end up paying their taxes.

"Certainly, it's a way to put pressure on people to pay those outstanding taxes, and that's basically the function of it, for what it's worth," he said.

That seems to be the case for the property on Windsor Street, where a man who identified himself as the owner exited the house, causing the entire structure to rattle as he closed the door.

The resident, who declined to give his name, said he was aware his home was going on the auction block.

The property was, he said, his family home, while acknowledging that its ramshackle condition made living there "a challenge."

But he brushed off any concern about it being sold out from under him.

"I have a year to pay it," he said of his tax bill.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Brieanna Charlebois, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says the results from last night’s U.S. midterm elections provide an opportunity for Canada to reset the relationship with its southern neighbour.
items.body:
Those at the top of Saskatchewan’s political establishment are treating last night’s U.S. midterms as the first step on the road to normalcy amid an ongoing trade war with Canada’s southern neighbour.

In a statement issued Wednesday morning, Premier Scott Moe said he believes the effect of U.S. tariffs on both sides of the border factored into the results.

“Last night’s U.S. election results were due at least in part to the impact of those harmful tariff policies,” Moe wrote.

  • Download the CTV News app to get breaking news alerts sent to your device

The premier went on to say the election results represent an opening for trade negotiations.

“We now have an opportunity to reset our relationship with the U.S. and restore free and fair trade between our two countries,” Moe wrote.

“I know Canada is ready to do this. Hopefully, the U.S. is as well.”

Tuesday’s midterms saw the Republicans lose substantial ground. As of 12 p.m. Wednesday, Democrats had seized 54 senate seats and 232 seats in the house, therefore capturing a majority in both chambers.

Finance Minister and Deputy Premier Jim Reiter spoke to reporters following question period and echoed the premier’s sentiments.

“I just hope that a message has been sent,” he said. “... As I said earlier, cost of living on both sides of the border is an issue, and the tariffs are a big part of that. So hopefully, common sense will prevail, and we’ll get some sort of an agreement soon.”

In her own statement, NDP Leader Carla Beck noted the relationship between Canada and the U.S. will not be repaired overnight but hoped Tuesday’s electoral results represented the beginning of the end for the “era of Donald Trump’s tariffs.”

“I believe last night’s election results were a stunning rebuke of these harmful economic policies and a clear message that the majority of Americans value their relationship with Canada and that they see us as allies, not enemies,” she wrote.

“We will never be the 51st state. We will always be a willing and active partner in economic prosperity. This is Canada, the True North, Strong and Free.”

items.title: Here's what fiscal hawks are watching out for in Budget 2026
items.description: The Liberal government is getting ready to reveal how a prolonged global energy shock and a series of spending commitments over the summer have affected the state of federal finances.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Finance and National Revenue Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne listens to a question during an armchair discussion at the Canadian Club of Ottawa, in Ottawa, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Liberal government is getting ready to reveal how a prolonged global energy shock and a series of spending commitments over the summer have affected the state of federal finances.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- The Liberal government is getting ready to reveal how a prolonged global energy shock and a series of spending commitments over the summer have affected the state of federal finances.

Budget 2026 -- the second federal budget tabled under Prime Minister Mark Carney -- is coming on Thursday.

Titled “Maitre Chez Nous” -- Masters of our Destiny -- the budget is expected to continue pivoting the federal government away from day-to-day government program spending and toward an aggressive infrastructure agenda.

Analysts will be looking for signs the federal government is keeping federal debt on a sustainable track as it tries to stoke investment and find new markets for trade.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan said in a new economic and fiscal outlook last month that her office is skeptical that Ottawa will meet its fiscal anchors.

The federal government has pledged to decrease the size of the deficit as a share of the economy in future years, and to balance the operating side of the budget by 2027-28.

The PBO expects deficit-to-GDP to instead rise midway through Ottawa’s horizon. The fiscal watchdog also says the operating budget could be balanced a year late; the Liberals claim they’re a year ahead of schedule.

Randall Bartlett, deputy chief economist at Desjardins, said it’s particularly difficult to estimate Ottawa’s deficits now, in large part because this government is often less clear than its predecessors were about spending timelines and classifications.

Seemingly arbitrary definitions for operating expenses and capital spending have become sources of irritation for fiscal hawks like Bartlett and the PBO.

“I think whether governments are borrowing to spend on operating expenses or capital investments does make a big difference,” Bartlett said.

“However, the federal government’s definition of capital versus operating is unclear, erroneous and, quite frankly, self-interested.”

According to Desjardins’ account, the federal government has added roughly $50 billion in planned new spending over the coming decade since April’s spring economic update.

Ottawa’s biggest new fiscal commitments in recent months include the planned Pacific Link oil pipeline to the B.C. coast and a new expanded tax incentive called the “productivity mega-deduction.”

The government also has substantial defence spending commitments on the horizon to meet rising NATO targets.

But Ottawa’s bottom line is getting a lift from stronger than expected nominal GDP -- a broad measure of Canada’s tax base. Counter-tariffs on U.S. imports are also feeding into federal coffers, while higher global oil prices from the war in the Middle East have been good for the government’s revenue stream.

Bartlett said he expects to see Ottawa’s deficits come in lower over the near term, thanks largely to the energy windfall. But he also warned that those revenues are not sustainable -- and the federal government will have to show it can be prudent once the well dries up.

“As oil prices start to fade going forward, when that tide goes out, we’re going to see who’s not wearing their swimsuit,” he said.

The federal government projected a deficit of $65.3 billion for fiscal 2026-27 in its spring economic statement, declining to $53.2 billion by 2030-31.

The PBO’s latest outlook has this year’s deficit $2 billion lower than that, at $63.3 billion. But the office sees the deficit fluctuating in the years ahead and ending up at $67.8 billion by 2030-31.

The PBO says if the government had not made those spending commitments since the spring, deficits would have been $4.6 billion lower per year over the forecast horizon.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne told reporters in Montreal on Wednesday that running deeper deficits to support workers in tariff-hit sectors is “the right thing to do.”

“If you want to be strong, you have to support people in industries and sectors and regions which have done nothing wrong,” he said.

“The fact that we have the strongest fiscal position in the G7 is exactly providing us the wherewithal to weather more difficult times, to support families, to support industry, and to build that bridge for the future.”

Champagne often compares Canada’s fiscal standing to that of other G7 partners to justify further borrowing and an aggressive infrastructure agenda.

Colin Busby, director of policy engagement at the C.D. Howe Institute, said while it’s true Canada is not in the same bleak fiscal situation as peer countries like the United Kingdom or France, he argued Ottawa ought not to take that for granted.

“The current trajectory that Canada is on, we have to be cautious that in five or ten years’ time, we could become like them if we don’t correct course,” he said.

The Liberals have downgraded the government’s previous fiscal anchor of a declining debt-to-GDP ratio, but many fiscal watchers -- including the PBO and the International Monetary Fund -- continue to see that ratio as an important marker of sustainable borrowing.

Desjardins sees this metric rising as the oil windfall fades starting in fiscal 2027-28, but predicts it will decline over the longer term.

Canada isn’t putting its sovereign credit rating at risk yet, Bartlett said, but additional spending could put Ottawa on a more precarious fiscal footing.

The federal government has used up much of its fiscal leeway with recent spending commitments, limiting its ability to respond to future shocks, he argued.

“There’s a real challenge for the federal government at this point, because it has painted itself into a bit of a fiscal corner as to what it can announce further going forward.”

Busby said he’s looking for a commitment from Ottawa to redouble its efforts to find savings in the budget.

The Liberals announced in last year’s budget that they were planning on $60 billion in savings from government spending over five years, a target Busby dismissed as “timid.”

“As we’re looking to pay for some of the bigger-ticket items ... are we going about ensuring that we’re getting the best value for money out of the programs that we have currently on offer?” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.title: Laval man guilty of eight real estate fraud counts in Quebec
items.description: A Montreal fraudster secretly registered 18% mortgages on homes he promised to buy outright
items.content: <p>A Montreal fraudster secretly registered 18% mortgages on homes he promised to buy outright</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639294101662986809.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A Montreal fraudster secretly registered 18% mortgages on homes he promised to buy outright
items.body:
A Laval, Quebec, man has been convicted of eight fraud counts at the Montreal courthouse following a scheme in which he secretly registered high-interest mortgages on properties he had agreed to purchase, leaving homeowners unable to recover what they were owed.

Quebec Court Judge Julie Riendeau found Constantin Niphakis, 46, of Laval, guilty of eight out of 10 fraud charges arising from real estate transactions between 2016 and 2018.

Niphakis had run a campaign using the slogan “J’achète des maisons CA$H” — meaning “I pay cash for homes” — targeting sellers who Montreal police described as often in a vulnerable situation.

Victim losses exceeded $1.1 million, including one who lost more than $240,000. Sentencing is set to begin in December.

Hidden mortgages, abandoned properties

In six of the eight cases, Niphakis had entered notarised agreements to purchase, renovate, and resell a home within a year.

Instead, he registered mortgages on those properties at rates as high as 18% without notifying the original owners, and made no mortgage payments, paid no municipal taxes, and paid no insurance costs, according to the judgment.

In two further cases, properties he agreed to renovate before resale were left in worse condition; in one, the vendor returned to find the doors open “and that feathers, hair and feces were scattered throughout the interior,” Judge Riendeau noted in her decision.

An Ontario mortgage broker has agreed to pay a $40,000 penalty after admitting to multiple regulatory breaches, including allowing an unlicensed referral agent to handle client intake and providing false or deceptive information to lenders. https://t.co/fXKBX6Pqj7 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 19, 2026

Victims describe the lasting toll

Prosecutor Rami El-Maoula was clear on intent.

“The evidence has shown beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Niphakis made false representations because he never intended to pay back the victims what was due to them,” he said.

Carol Ringrose, who had been fleeing an abusive relationship in 2016 when she sought a quick sale, described the full extent of the loss: “I lost my home. I lost everything. I ended up living with friends on couches and everything until I could get settled. And I’m renting a room.”

Eugene Saint-Germain, who had inherited a home from his sister and approached Niphakis after hearing his radio advertisement, reflected on the years it took to reach a verdict: “Finally, justice. It took a long time. Ten years is a long time.”

The case arrives amid broader industry concern about real estate fraud across Canada.

Lauren van den Berg, President and Chief Executive Officer of Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) in Toronto, previously said that “mortgage fraud not only undermines trust, it drives up housing costs for everyone.”

The Niphakis conviction is not an isolated case in Quebec. In May, four men were arrested in Montreal and Quebec City in a $4.5-million real estate fraud probe in which the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) alleged the group targeted financially distressed homeowners across approximately 20 incidents.

They lured them through online ads offering debt relief before victims “unknowingly signed documents transferring ownership of their property.”

Judge Riendeau’s ruling in the Niphakis case left no room for the argument that the scheme was a business venture gone wrong.

“It is the same repetition of the same conduct in multiple transactions that satisfy the court that the accused’s conduct cannot be viewed as a business venture that went wrong or as mere negligence,” she wrote.

Charges against co-accused Mark Blumenthal, 55, of Côte-St-Luc, Quebec, were withdrawn earlier in 2026.

items._ogDesc: Greater Toronto real estate prices have plunged 28.4% from peak levels. Weak sales and high inventory keep the region in a buyer's market.
items.body:
Greater Toronto real estate prices have now seen the largest correction in history. That didn’t stop prices from slipping further in October, according to TRREB data. Lofty inventory and weak sales pushed prices down to their lowest level in almost 6 years.

Toronto Real Estate Prices Have Plunged 28.4% Since Peak

The price of a typical home across Greater Toronto.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a home across Greater Toronto slipped 0.13% (-$1.2k) to $915,400 in October, 4.3% (-$40.8k) lower than last year. Home prices have plunged 28.4% (-$363.4k) since peaking in 2022. Even the sharpest correction in the region’s history has yet to wipe out pandemic gains though. Prices are back to December 2020 levels, though many would argue this is a modelling issue. Weak demand may confirm that, as buyers clearly don’t see this level as a “deal.”

Toronto Home Sales Fall To 3 Year Low

Greater Toronto home sales through the MLS.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Sales suffered another setback last month. TRREB reported 5,600 sales through the MLS in October, down 7.9% from last year. This is the second year to show a year-over-year drop in sales, marking a 3-year low for the month. Last month’s demand wasn’t the worst in the slump, but pre-pandemic volumes hadn’t been this low since 2008. Not the worst, but certainly far from anything that resembles normal.

Fewer New Listings, But The Volume Remains Historically Strong

New listings provided something for Toronto real estate bulls to chew on. There were 14,170 new listings in October, 11.9% lower than last year. The slide also marked the weakest October since 2022, though there’s no need to fear a shortage. Despite being the slowest volume for the month in 4 years, only 8 of the past 22 years have seen more new listings.

The sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) only came in at 37.9% in October. That means TRREB is still in a buyer’s market, where the industry expects prices to fall further.

Toronto Real Estate Inventory Pulls Back, Third Highest On Record

Greater Toronto active listings of homes for sale in October.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

One reason for the weak inflow of new listings may be the lofty levels of inventory sitting on the market. There were 25,100 active listings for sale in October, down 10% from last year but the third-most ever. The year-over-year drop was sharp, but it’s from the record high for October.

Greater Toronto real estate doesn’t look like it’s set to exit its tailspin soon. The prolonged correction is working at a snail’s pace, spending 4 years to roll back roughly 14 months of gains. With experts warning of higher rates and a wobbly economy, any mitigating factors seem beyond the horizon.

items.title: Rate hike and election drag Vancouver home sales down
items.description: Benchmark prices slid as buyers held back across Metro Vancouver’s housing market
items.content: <p>Benchmark prices slid as buyers held back across Metro Vancouver’s housing market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639294072149981449.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Benchmark prices slid as buyers held back across Metro Vancouver’s housing market
items.body:
Metro Vancouver’s residential market retreated in October, with sales dropping 10.2% year-over-year and landing 22.5% below the 10-year seasonal average, according to data from the Greater Vancouver REALTORS (GVR).

The GVR reported 2,024 transactions last month, against 2,255 in October 2025.

New listings fell 11.6% to 4,805, 1% above the 10-year seasonal average, while total active inventory dipped 4.3% to 15,688, still 24% above the long-term benchmark.

Andrew Lis, GVR chief economist and vice-president of data analytics in Vancouver, attributed the pullback to external forces piling on an already subdued market.

“October came with a few suspenseful distractions for buyers and sellers alike, with a somewhat surprising Bank of Canada rate hike and a snap provincial election among them,” Lis said.

“Between the onslaught of news coverage of the provincial and municipal elections, and the uncertainty surrounding where mortgage rates may be headed, it’s not entirely surprising that market participants took a step back in October to recalibrate.”

Prices keep sliding across Metro Vancouver

The MLS Home Price Index composite benchmark fell to $1,068,600 in October, down 5.2% from October 2025 and 0.7% from September.

Detached homes led losses — the benchmark dropped 7% to $1,775,200 on 643 sales.

Apartment transactions declined 16.7% to 892, with the benchmark off 5.9% at $673,400.

Attached homes were steadier, with 468 sales and a benchmark of $1,006,500, down 5.5% year-over-year.

The overall sales-to-active listings ratio sat at 13.4% — with detached at 11.6%, attached at 16.5%, and apartments at 13.5%.

Historical data shows downward price pressure typically builds when the ratio holds below 12% over a sustained period.

Read more: GTA home sales stumble in October as buyers seek economic clarity

Rate hike reshapes broker conversations

The Bank of Canada’s 25-basis-point move to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, added fresh urgency to what the BoC’s next decision means for the mortgage market.

For brokers already working through Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal wave, the timing was unwelcome.

Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright, a Toronto-based digital real estate law platform, was direct: “A rate hike likely locks us into year-over-year declines in housing activity for the rest of this year and into next, and I don’t see things turning until there’s a rate drop.”

His practical advice to clients approaching renewal: “If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up.”

Read more: Calgary home sales fall as condo oversupply presses prices lower

Lis, meanwhile, identified one potential tailwind.

“With one quarter-point rate hike now behind us, and financial markets pricing in a slight chance of another quarter-point hike in December, it’s possible some buyers may step in to take advantage of rate holds that will soon be expiring,” he said.

“Still, it’s a difficult quandary for buyers who’ve watched prices edge lower throughout the year, only to see those affordability gains eroded by higher borrowing costs.”

Whether the market ends 2026 on firmer ground, he added, “remains the defining question that will set the tone for the New Year.”

items.title: Here’s where Canada’s new condo prices fell hardest in Q3
items.description: Statistics Canada tracks where developer prices are sliding and where they’re gaining ground
items.content: <p>Statistics Canada tracks where developer prices are sliding and where they’re gaining ground</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/ca/046/0348_637393692045334697.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Statistics Canada tracks where developer prices are sliding and where they’re gaining ground
items.body:
Developer prices for newly built condominium apartments fell 0.6% nationally in Q3 2026, according to Statistics Canada’s New Condominium Apartment Price Index (NCAPI).

The decline was driven largely by softening in Toronto and Vancouver, two markets that together represent more than 80% of the nine-city composite.

Victoria recorded the steepest quarterly drop in the country at 1.8%, followed by Vancouver at 1.0% and Toronto at 0.8%.

Edmonton and Calgary also declined, by 0.7% and 0.3% respectively.

The NCAPI measures changes in developers’ selling prices for comparable units in newly built apartment-style condominiums; it does not capture resale prices or movements in the average sale price.

The release arrives as Canada’s mortgage brokers continue working through a condo correction that few believe has fully run its course.

Dan Eisner, founder and chief executive of True North Mortgage in Canada, previously told Canadian Mortgage Professional that nothing yet suggests a turning point is at hand.

“I don’t see a bottom yet,” Eisner said.

“If the Canadian government came out and said, ‘We’re increasing immigration back to the levels seen under [former Prime Minister] Trudeau,’ then I would say, ‘OK, we’re going to see a bottom.’ But I don’t see that.”

New Condominium Apartment Price Index, Q3 2026 — Statistics Canada

New Condominium Apartment Price Index — Q3 2026 (base: 2017 = 100)

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0273-01, released November 3, 2026. Index measures developers' selling prices for newly built apartment-style condominiums; excludes resale prices.

Victoria and Vancouver drive western weakness

Canada’s west coast condo markets have emerged as the weakest in the country for developer pricing.

Victoria’s 1.8% quarterly fall led all nine cities tracked by Statistics Canada, while Vancouver – a dominant force in the national composite – fell 1.0%.

For brokers navigating the ongoing correction in Toronto’s new condo prices and sales activity, the gap between original purchase prices and current appraised values has become a defining challenge.

Eisner explained the bind facing owners who are underwater on their mortgages.

“Now for a lot of people, especially condo owners who are underwater in their mortgage, option one is off the table,” he told CMP.

“Because if they sell, they don’t get their money back. And then they still owe money on the mortgage afterwards which means that the lender won’t release title.”

Shaun Hildebrand of Urbanation says bulk purchases and investment groups helped drive a second consecutive quarterly increase in GTHA new condo sales, while concerns continue to grow over a shrinking development pipeline and future housing supply shortages https://t.co/SjEeyvaIV4 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 22, 2026

Ottawa and Montreal offer rare bright spots

Ottawa was the strongest market in the nine-city index during Q3 2026, posting a 1.6% gain.

Montreal added 0.7%, while Halifax and Quebec City were unchanged.

The regional divergence is consistent with what the Bank of Canada identified as an inventory overhang of small condominiums restraining new construction across the country’s major centres.

For Taz Zaide of 6ix Mortgage Group in Ontario, the Q3 2026 numbers echo what he is already seeing on the ground. He previously shared with CMP that appraisal shortfalls continue to steer clients away from condo transactions entirely.

“Especially on the appraisal front, we’re finding that people are still bleeding on that end. So we don’t think the condo market will be reversing anytime soon,” Zaide said.

“And we haven’t seen that many people buying condos as of late. It looks like people are trying to steer away from them, knowing this as well. Most of our transactions have been anything but a condo.”

items.body:
VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days.

Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.

But with an official BC Assessment valuation of more than $1.7 million, the house could represent a bargain when it goes up for sale at Vancouver’s annual tax auction at city hall on Wednesday with a reserve price of just $72,051.

It is among more than 60 properties that were auctioned off in this year’s City of Vancouver tax sale, set off by owners who have not paid their taxes for three years in a row, with the reserve, or upset price, set at the amount owed to the city.

If East Vancouver is not to your taste, then perhaps Point Grey Road? It’s one of the most exclusive addresses in Canada, where neighbours include Lululemon billionaire Chip Wilson, whose $73-million home is the most valuable in B.C.

A few blocks down the road from Wilson are two side-by-side houses valued around $5 million and $6 million. They are steps from Jericho Beach and the Royal Vancouver Yacht Club, and sold for about half their value at $2 million and $2.75 million.

There is, of course, a catch.

After auction day, the current owners have a year to redeem their property by paying their taxes, resulting in a refund to the bidder, plus interest.

Ron Usher, a retired notary public, said tax auctions are “not for the faint of heart or the inexperienced.”

“I suspect some of these tax sales are more whoops than deliberate,” Usher said, citing situations such as inheritances.

“You can imagine the law is very much structured to give the maximum possible opportunity for the owner to sort out the problem,” Usher said.

Though a posting last week included 116 properties listed for auction, by the time it began at 10 a.m. Wednesday, only 66 remained. Owners of three more properties paid their taxes while the auction was ongoing and the homes were removed from the block.

Vancouverite Darius Wu attended the auction “mostly for fun, hoping I’d get a bargain.”

The 30-year-old likened the auction to buying a lottery ticket, but better.

“In a lottery, you lose money no matter what. Here, I would say, the odds are probably one in a hundred. You don’t lose any money, and if you win, it’s still … pretty good.”

It was Wu’s first auction in Vancouver, but he ducked out before noon after concluding he wouldn’t outbid others in attendance.

“I think there are way more serious people here,” he said, noting many of the bids were climbing to around half of the property value listed. “You need a lot of cash to actually participate here.”

As the auction dragged on, the dozens of people who had earlier jockeyed for a spot inside the chambers trickled out, with the attendees dwindling to about a dozen.

Among the few left by its conclusion was one man who won bids on dozens of properties, including the one home on Windsor Street. Though he declined an interview, he said he didn’t expect to be transferred the property, and would instead collect the interest.

If the owner eventually pays the tax, the bidder is refunded the upset fee with interest of six per cent. But if it is not redeemed by its owner within the year, the bidder must pay the balance of their bid within 30 days.

Sean Holden, a longtime Vancouver Realtor, called bidding at the auction “an exercise in futility.”

He said he often steers clients away from the auction. When asked if he has ever attended himself, his response is quick.

“I wouldn’t waste my time,” he said through a chuckle.

Holden points out that tax auction sales that go through to completion are very rare.

But they do happen, both in Vancouver and other B.C. municipalities that conduct their auctions every September on properties with two years of unpaid taxes.

Three properties have changed hands in the last five years in Burnaby, while the City of Vancouver said in a statement that there “were only three instances in the last 10 years where a property changed hands from a tax sale.”

“The property taxes on almost all properties have historically been paid within the one-year redemption period,” the statement said.

The City of Vancouver tells potential buyers not to trespass, but recommends people do their own research before bidding, noting in a posting last week that it is not responsible for the condition or quality of the homes.

“Prospective purchasers are urged to research the properties and make all necessary inquiries to municipal and other government departments to determine the existence of any bylaws, restriction, charges or other conditions which may affect the value or suitability of the properties,” it says.

Holden, who has been a Realtor in the city for about three decades, said that adds risk for the buyer.

“You don’t know what condition it will be, and (if) the sellers are forced out by the bank, whether they knock holes in the wall or do other strange things. You’re taking a huge risk,” he said.

All properties auctioned on Wednesday were bid on. Only one property was sold for the upset price, but that amounted to nearly $1 million.

The two properties listed for sale in Burnaby last year both went through.

The minutes from the tax sale show the same person purchased both properties.

An empty 9,262-square-foot lot on Walker Avenue sold for the upset price of $845, while its assessed value is $37,700.

The other property, which had an upset price of $269, was sold to the same buyer for $5,000. That may be less of a bargain — the property measures just 94-square feet and has a valuation of $3,600.

The City of Burnaby confirmed both properties were transferred after the one-year redemption period expired.

The City of Kelowna said it had an average of “about three to four properties” sold at its auction over the past six years, but added that “actual transfers of ownership through this process are very rare.”

“City staff recall the last transfer occurring around 2016/2017,” a spokeswoman said in a statement.

Abbotsford did not auction any properties this year or in 2024, but in 2025, it had two properties on the block. One sale went through on what the city called “a small undeveloped piece of land.”

The highest bidders from Wednesday’s auction must pay the upset price by noon Thursday.

Holden said bidders need to be prepared for their money to be tied up for a while, noting that while a six per cent interest rate may be enticing, most owners end up paying their taxes.

“Certainly, it’s a way to put pressure on people to pay those outstanding taxes, and that’s basically the function of it, for what it’s worth,” he said.

That seems to be the case for the property on Windsor Street, where a man who identified himself as the owner exited the house, causing the entire structure to rattle as he closed the door.

The resident, who declined to give his name, said he was aware his home was going on the auction block.

The property was, he said, his family home, while acknowledging that its ramshackle condition made living there “a challenge.”

But he brushed off any concern about it being sold out from under him.

“I have a year to pay it,” he said of his tax bill.

This report by Brieanna Charlebois, The Canadian Press, was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

items.description: Rate hike and trade fears pushed GTA buyers to the sidelines
items.content: <p>Rate hike and trade fears pushed GTA buyers to the sidelines</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639294019470753952.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rate hike and trade fears pushed GTA buyers to the sidelines
items.body:
Greater Toronto Area home sales fell 7.9% in October as buyers contended with the Bank of Canada’s first interest rate increase in three years, piling fresh anxiety atop existing concerns over Canada-US trade negotiations and persistent inflation.

Data from the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board (TRREB) in Ontario showed 5,603 homes sold across the GTA last month, a 7.9% year-over-year decline.

New listings fell 11.9% year-over-year to 14,173, while total active inventory across the region stood at 25,098 properties.

The average selling price declined 2.7% to $1,024,108, with TRREB’s Multiple Listing Service (MLS) Home Price Index Composite benchmark down 4.3% over the same period.

On a seasonally adjusted basis, both sales and new listings edged higher month-over-month compared with September. 

Borrowing costs cloud an already hesitant market

The Bank of Canada raised its overnight lending rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, and its first move in a year.

The decision reversed a prolonged pause even as GTA home sales had climbed 9.4% year over year in June before momentum faded through the summer and autumn.

Jason Mercer, chief information officer at TRREB in Ontario, said declining prices have provided a partial offset.

“GTA homebuyers continued to benefit from substantial negotiating power on price over the past year,” he said.

“While borrowing costs have increased on the back of higher inflation, the impact on monthly mortgage payments has been mitigated by lower selling prices, helping keep affordability in check.”

Aled ab Iorwerth of CMHC says greater certainty on trade could improve confidence among homebuyers and developers, supporting housing activity and construction at a time when higher rates and economic uncertainty continue to weigh on the market. https://t.co/3d7Cu3TCov — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 3, 2026

The broker view on the ground

For mortgage brokers working in the GTA, October’s figures reinforced a prolonged period of constrained client activity.

The challenges facing first-time homebuyers in Canada’s 2026 housing market have been particularly acute in Toronto, where lower prices have brought new complications of their own.

Toronto-based mortgage broker Micky Khaneka, who has spoken with Canadian Mortgage Professional about Toronto’s condo market remaining in limbo despite falling prices, described the bind clients face.

“People are starting to pick up resales or newbuilds that are being built for closing at a much, much lower price than what they were initially sold for,” he said.

“But the clients who bought at those prices are still in a little bit of limbo because unless there are blanket appraisals from the banks, it’s very challenging for them to get appraisals on them.”

TRREB President Daniel Steinfeld, also based in Toronto, pointed to international events as the most plausible route to renewed buyer confidence.

“If a Canada-U.S. trade deal is reached, GTA residents could gain a clearer picture of the economic outlook,” he said.

“Combined with a resolution to the conflict in the Middle East, this could help ease concerns about inflation and economic uncertainty, strengthen consumer confidence and renew interest in homeownership as we move into 2027.”

items.title: Canada, US dominate global AI talent: report
items.description: ‘The main constraint on AI adoption will not be tools or investment — but the availability of skilled professionals’
items.content: <p>‘The main constraint on AI adoption will not be tools or investment — but the availability of skilled professionals’</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0363_639293071848827900.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: ‘The main constraint on AI adoption will not be tools or investment — but the availability of skilled professionals’
items.body:
North America holds a commanding lead over the rest of the world in artificial intelligence (AI) talent, with the United States scoring a perfect 100 and Canada climbing to second place globally with a score of 58.345 — more than 20 points clear of any European economy — according to a new international index.

Every other country, including established technology powers –  such as Germany, the United Kingdom and Australia –  trails well behind.

The 2026 Global Workforce Specialization Index – produced by analytics firm Ataraxis – covers 32 countries and six professional fields. India is the only country that comes close to Canada, scoring 57.57, but it is edged out on the density and international readiness measures that matter most to employers hiring at scale. Germany, the next major contender, scores significantly lower still — underlining just how wide the gap is between North America and the rest of the world.

The US operates in a tier of its own. Canada leads every other country, but its score of 58.345 against the US perfect 100 reflects a gap that shapes hiring competition, compensation benchmarks and talent retention pressure for Canadian organisations daily.

How Canada earned second place

The Ataraxis index constructs its composite score from three weighted dimensions: absolute workforce capacity at 40%, capacity density relative to population at 35%, and service-delivery readiness at 25%. Those weightings explain why India, despite recording a higher absolute AI capacity score of 81.9 compared with Canada’s 54.7, does not hold second place. Canada’s capacity-density score of 39.9 substantially outpaces India’s 6.6, and both countries receive equivalent service-delivery readiness scores of 90.

Separate data from CBRE’s 2026 Scoring Tech Talent report reinforces the picture. The number of AI-skilled tech talent workers across the US and Canada increased by 45% year-over-year to 751,000 as of mid-2026, with AI-specialty talent clustered at 37% of the US total, while Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver contain 60% of Canada’s. Canada’s tech wage premium sits at just 8% above the national average, compared with 15% in the US, according to CBRE — a disparity that creates persistent pressure on Canadian employers competing for the same specialist pool as American firms.

Canada’s position builds on long-term investment in foundational research through institutions including Mila, the Vector Institute and the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii), which received a C$50 million, five-year provincial commitment in July 2026. The concentration of 60 per cent of Canada’s AI-specialty talent in three cities is a sign of depth, but it also means the country’s workforce advantage is geographically narrow, making those markets intensely competitive for recruiters. 

For HR leaders tracking Canada’s widening AI skills gap and the confidence levels of workers using these tools, the ranking underscores that talent density and talent retention are two separate problems.

What the ranking means for HR leaders

Workforce concentration does not automatically translate into broad commercial deployment. Statistics Canada’s Canadian Survey on Business Conditions, conducted from April to May 2026, found that 19.2% of businesses had used AI to produce goods or deliver services during the preceding 12 months — up from 6.1% in 2024, but still leaving most Canadian enterprises outside active adoption.

Patrick Poulin, President and Managing Director of Randstad Canada in Montreal, has identified the specialist shortage as the central constraint. “In 2026, the main constraint on AI adoption will not be tools or investment — but the availability of skilled professionals who can implement these systems at scale,” he said. Rob Wilmot, General Manager of IBM Consulting Canada in Toronto, echoed that view in February 2026, noting that Canadian organisations are entering 2026 “not because the economy is predictable, but because leaders are betting on AI as a long-term growth engine.”

HRD Canada’s reporting on how HR functions are excluded from AI strategy decisions at 37% of Canadian firms, according to an IBM study with Oxford Economics, suggests many organisations still lack the internal alignment needed to deploy that talent effectively. 

For those that do, HR leaders tracking the five workforce transformation priorities outlined in Canada’s national AI strategy will find the Ataraxis results both affirming and cautionary — Canada has the specialist depth to compete globally, but converting that into business-wide productivity gains requires deliberate action now.
